content_summary.point: Complementarity, land vs money: host frames Gesell as known for money and demurrage, who also worked on land and so is close to George; calls them 'the two blind spots of modern economics'.
content_summary.quote_le_50w: two blind spots of modern economics

content_summary.point: Guest: George came first on land; Gesell borrowed George's critiques of land appropriation and applied them to money issuance and banking.
content_summary.grep: applied a lot of that thinking to money

content_summary.point: Guest claims Gesell's main complaint against Georgism (beyond the standard ones) was that assessing land value (improved-parcel share) was too great a burden, which Detroit's assessment work has now removed. Unsourced; Freiland is not mentioned by name anywhere in the talk.
Detroit: land values cluster around downtown and parks (and possibly transit); a 261-parcel all-vacant speculator is taken from an unnamed article, not from the guest's analysis.
content_summary.quote_le_50w: owns 261 parcels, all of them vacant

content_summary.point: The central claim as actually spoken: log-scale value per acre, improved (blue) vs vacant (red); high-value vacant parcels 'sit the longest before they sell 60 years, 40 years' while improved parcels 'shift hands every three to six years'. The word 'waterfront' is not attached to the idle-parcel claim in the audio ('downtown rich land, riverfront land' is a guess at the chart); no counts, no sample, no source for the turnover figures; the guest says that part is 'missing from this figure'.
content_summary.quote_le_50w: 60 years, 40 years ... every three to six years

content_summary.point: Data source: 'recreated ... from the mayor's office data'; the mayor's office is said to have done the land/improvement assessment for most residential and commercial lots. No dataset name.

City-sourced figure: '74% of the parcels will pay less', said to come from Detroit's own publications (not checked here; the wiki's Detroit page cites a 17% average homeowner cut from the city plan instead).
content_summary.quote_le_50w: 74% of the parcels will pay less

content_summary.point: Tools the mayor's office is said to need: interactive mouse-over maps and a millage 'pilot seat' to tune and administer an LVT ('flying blind' without them).
content_summary.quote_le_50w: flying blind if you don't have tools like this

content_summary.point: Industrial parcels 'pretty much except for a handful will pay more' under the plan (guest's reading of the city's map).

uncertainties: (1) Whisper small/medium can mishear numbers; the 60/40/3-6 figures were consistent across both models. (2) The audio is an edited excerpt of a live webinar, so unseen slides may hold counts the speaker did not say; none could be recovered. (3) The queue's 'prime waterfront land idle 40-60 years' paraphrase is stronger than the spoken text. (4) The 'great paper that came out this month' (09:04-09:30) and the article cited for the 261-parcel speculator are unidentified. (5) The Gesell-on-assessment-burden claim is the guest's gloss and was not checked against Gesell's text. (6) Mismatch between RSS duration (18:30) and the downloaded file (about 21 min) is due to inserted ads; ad copy appears at 00:00-00:48, 02:51-03:50, 19:36-20:32 and should be ignored. (7) Guest identity and affiliation beyond the HGSS blurb could not be verified.
